name: Fractional laser resurfacing

lead: Fractional laser resurfacing uses a laser that treats a grid of microscopic columns of skin and leaves the tissue between them intact. It is offered by dermatologists and plastic surgeons for acne scars, other scars, wrinkles, sun damage and uneven texture.

In looksmaxxing communities it sits in the clinic-based 'hardmaxx' tier of skin treatment. Forum users describe it as a stronger option than at-home skincare, and some report that recovery is harder than expected.

paras: Ablative lasers (such as CO2 and erbium) vaporize microscopic channels of skin, while non-ablative fractional lasers heat the tissue without removing it. The resulting controlled injury is described in the literature as stimulating new collagen and remodeling of the dermis. Because only a fraction of the surface is treated each time, healing is faster than with older fully ablative resurfacing.

Reported adverse effects include redness, swelling, crusting, acne flares, herpes simplex reactivation, pigment changes and scarring. Dermatology reviews describe skin phototyping (the Fitzpatrick scale) as relevant to predicting outcomes of procedures such as laser resurfacing. Treatments are performed by licensed clinicians; devices are regulated medical devices in most jurisdictions.

lead: Fractional laser resurfacing is a cosmetic and medical procedure in which a laser delivers energy to the skin in a pattern of many microscopic zones, leaving untreated skin between them. It is used for scars (especially atrophic acne scars), wrinkles, sun-damaged skin, stretch marks and uneven texture, and is a form of the broader category of laser skin resurfacing. [1][2]

Fractional devices come in two main kinds. Ablative systems, typically CO2 or erbium lasers, vaporize tissue in the treated columns; non-ablative systems, such as the 1550 nm devices marketed as Fraxel, heat the dermis without removing the surface. [1][3] Fractional treatment was developed after earlier fully ablative CO2 resurfacing, which produced notable results but also high complication rates. [3][4]

Clinical studies, consensus reports and randomized trials support fractional laser treatment for several scar types, with improvement typically gradual over multiple sessions. Reported adverse effects include prolonged redness, pigment changes, infection and scarring, and downtime for ablative treatments is several days. [5][6][7] Forum users on looksmax.org discuss it as a clinic option within skin-focused looksmaxxing and describe heavy downtime. [8]

paras: Laser resurfacing is divided into ablative methods, which vaporize tissue and create a wound, and non-ablative methods, which leave the skin surface intact. Fractional delivery places many small treated zones per area of skin with healthy tissue between them, which is intended to speed healing compared with treating the whole surface. [9][3]

Reviews of the field describe a spectrum running from non-ablative fractional lasers, through ablative fractional CO2 and erbium devices, to fully ablative resurfacing, with a trade-off between degree of change and recovery time. [3]

Clinicians commonly classify skin by the Fitzpatrick scale, which is based on tendency to burn and tan, because it relates to the risk of photodamage and to outcomes after procedures such as laser resurfacing and chemical peeling. [10] A registered trial of a 1550 nm fractional laser for acne scars was specifically designed for Fitzpatrick types IV to VI. [11]

Laser resurfacing began in the 1980s with continuous-wave CO2 lasers, whose high rate of side effects including scarring led to the development of short-pulse, rapidly scanned CO2 lasers and erbium:YAG lasers. [3] A 1996 study of pulsed CO2 resurfacing in 111 perioral and periorbital areas reported clinical improvement in photoaged skin, and a 1998 evaluation of 500 patients catalogued complications of the technique. [12][4]

A 2007 study applied fractional photothermolysis to atrophic scars. [13] A 2014 consensus report addressed laser treatment of traumatic scars with an emphasis on ablative fractional resurfacing. [14] A 2008 report on 961 fractional treatments described the side-effect profile of the newer technique. [15]

Human studies cover several indications. A randomized trial compared fractional CO2 laser with carboxytherapy for stretch marks. [16] Fractional CO2 has been studied for acne scarring, where a 2008 report described successful treatment of acneiform scars, and for burn scars, where a 2022 review concluded laser therapy is superior to topical treatments and can be combined with surgery. [17][18]

Randomized and controlled trials have tested fractional laser combined with other treatments, including a split-face trial of an antioxidant serum after non-ablative fractional laser in a Chinese population, a trial of fractional CO2 followed by photodynamic therapy for actinic keratosis, and combinations with platelet-rich plasma, hyaluronic acid and botulinum toxin. [19][20][21][22][23] A randomized trial of fractionated laser on aged skin was also run to test whether it could reduce later actinic neoplasia, with related trials registered. [24][25]

Complication data come mostly from case series: the 500-patient CO2 series and the 961-treatment fractional series. [4][15] Trials registered on ClinicalTrials.gov include studies of a 2910 nm laser for perioral lines and of self-harm scars. [26][27]

Reported effects after fractional or ablative resurfacing include erythema, swelling, crusting, acne eruptions, herpes simplex outbreaks, changes in pigmentation and scarring. [15][4][9] CO2 lasers have been described as carrying a greater risk of hypopigmentation and scarring than erbium lasers because of greater heat generation. [9]

A 2023 review of chemical peels characterized lasers as having proved inadequate for some deep perioral lines, in contrast to deep peels. [28] A review of burn scars notes that the use of lasers in hospital dermatology departments remains limited. [18]

Fractional resurfacing appears in looksmax.org discussions as a clinic-based treatment for skin. One user described having CO2 resurfacing and being unable to go outside or exercise for about a week afterward, and said three sessions had been recommended. [8] Other posters in the same thread discussed laser hair removal and intense pulsed light as skin-improvement options. [8] Users also list laser resurfacing as one of several procedures bundled in surgery trips abroad.

Ongoing registered trials examine fractional laser as prophylaxis against actinic keratosis and non-melanoma skin cancer in older skin, laser-induced rejuvenation mechanisms, and newer wavelengths. [24][25][26][29]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, fractional laser is discussed as a stronger clinic alternative to skincare, with posters trading accounts of the downtime and the number of sessions needed. [8]

claims.claim: Clinic laser resurfacing meaningfully improves scars and skin texture.
Recovery is brutal and needs about a week off.
Lasers and light treatments such as IPL give long-lasting better skin overall.
Laser resurfacing can be safely bundled into multi-procedure trips abroad.
